set1.q: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma cells express which pair of cluster of differentiation markers?
opts: Coexpression of cluster of differentiation 19 and 5 identifies chronic lymphocytic leukemia on flow cytometry. Tell: 19 and 5 are the leukemia; 15 and 30 are Hodgkin.
Cluster of differentiation 20 is the rituximab target on B cells and 5 is part of the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair. Tell: classical Hodgkin is 15 and 30.
Cluster of differentiation 19 belongs to the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair (with 5). Tell: Hodgkin pairs 30 with 15.

Correct. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses cluster of differentiation 15 and cluster of differentiation 30. The diagnosis itself is made by excisional lymph node biopsy, avoiding fine needle aspiration.

set1.q: Which presentation fits primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma?
opts: Widespread red itchy erythroderma is Sezary syndrome, a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Tell: a mediastinal B-cell lymphoma is a chest mass.
Blurred vision and headache come from immunoglobulin M hyperviscosity in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: thick blood blurs vision; a mediastinal mass causes cough.

Correct. Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphomas present with a large mediastinal mass, cough and an abnormal chest X-ray. Central nervous system lymphoma, by contrast, presents with headaches, lethargy and neurologic deficits.
Headaches, lethargy and neurologic deficits that mirror primary brain tumors describe central nervous system lymphoma. Tell: mediastinal disease shows in the chest.

set1.q: At what rate does monoclonal B lymphocytosis progress to chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Monoclonal B lymphocytosis, a count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms, progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at a rate of 1-2% per year.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma to multiple myeloma. Tell: 10% belongs to smoldering myeloma; 1-2% to monoclonal B lymphocytosis.
A quarter per year overstates the risk; monoclonal B lymphocytosis progresses at only 1-2% per year. Tell: it is a low-risk precursor.
Above 50% within 2 years is the risk in some high-risk smoldering myeloma groups, not the yearly rate for monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: 1-2% per year here.

set1.q: In the Lugano staging of lymphoma, involved lymph node regions both above and below the diaphragm are which stage?
opts: Stage 1 is localized disease, a single lymph node region or a single organ. Tell: more than one region crossing the diaphragm is beyond stage 1.
Stage 2 is two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm. Tell: crossing the diaphragm moves it to stage 3.

Correct. In the Lugano classification (a modified Ann Arbor system), stage 3 is two or more lymph node regions above and below the diaphragm. Stage 2 keeps them on the same side; stage 4 is widespread disease in multiple organs.
Stage 4 is widespread disease with multiple organs involved, with or without nodes. Tell: nodes on both sides without organ spread stop at stage 3.

set1.q: Which is a listed risk factor for non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
opts: Iron deficiency is not on the risk factor list; the list centers on immune problems, prior cancer treatment, exposures and chronic infections. Tell: immune suppression, not a nutrient deficiency.

Correct. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk factors include immunosuppression, prior transplantation, prior chemotherapy or radiation, autoimmune conditions, Crohn's disease, farming exposures, chronic infections, male sex, White race and family history.
Male gender, not female, is the listed risk factor for non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: the sex risk is male.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common in developed countries. Tell: the risk runs toward developed, not developing, countries.

set1.q: Which T-cell lymphoma often affects the nasal region?
opts: Correct. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma often affects the nasal region. It is one of the diverse T-cell lymphomas, alongside peripheral T-cell (most common), anaplastic large cell and hepatosplenic types.
Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma is named for the liver and spleen, not the nose. Tell: the nasal one is extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma.
Intestinal T-cell lymphomas involve the bowel. Tell: a nasal mass points to the extranodal natural killer/T-cell type.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, is the most common T-cell lymphoma (one third of cases) but is not tied to the nose. Tell: most common is peripheral; nasal is extranodal natural killer/T-cell.

set1.q: Sporadic Burkitt lymphoma is almost always seen below which age?
opts: Twenty is too young a cut-off; the sporadic type is almost always seen below age 35. Tell: young adults up to their mid-30s are included.
Correct. Sporadic Burkitt lymphoma is typically seen in the United States and Western Europe, more in males, and almost always below age 35. That makes it a disease of children and young adults.
Fifty is too high; sporadic Burkitt is almost always below 35. Tell: Burkitt is a disease of the young.
Age over 60 is a poor prognostic factor in non-Hodgkin lymphoma and the older Hodgkin peak, not the sporadic Burkitt cut-off. Tell: sporadic Burkitt is under 35.

set1.q: How is a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated?
opts: Correct. Management depends heavily on subtype and presentation; a single-node, non-aggressive lymphoma is treated with radiation. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas instead get multi-drug chemotherapy with rituximab.
Multi-drug chemotherapy is the approach to aggressive B-cell lymphomas. Tell: one node and non-aggressive means radiation.
Autologous transplant improves survival in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma. Tell: transplant belongs to myeloma; a single indolent node gets radiation.
Allopurinol and fluids prevent tumor lysis syndrome before aggressive lymphoma treatment; they do not treat the lymphoma. Tell: prevention, not therapy.

set1.q: What is the backbone of treatment for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma?
opts: Rituximab with multi-drug chemotherapy is the aggressive B-cell lymphoma regimen. Tell: plasma cell disease uses a proteasome inhibitor backbone.
Novel cellular therapy as first treatment
Novel therapies, including cellular therapies and bispecific antibodies, are currently used for relapsed myeloma. Tell: they are kept for relapse, not first-line.
Proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory drug and steroid

Correct. Newly diagnosed patients are treated with a 3- or 4-drug regimen built on a proteasome inhibitor and immunomodulatory drug backbone with steroids. Transplant candidates add autologous transplant and maintenance.
Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor given continuously
Continuous Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor monotherapy is a chronic lymphocytic leukemia approach. Tell: myeloma starts on proteasome inhibitor, immunomodulatory drug and steroid.

set1.topic: MGUS and smoldering myeloma
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set1.q: An M-protein of 1.5 g/dL, clonal marrow plasma cells of 4% and no anemia, bone lesions or renal failure fit which disorder?
opts: Smoldering myeloma needs an M-protein above 3 g/dL and 10-60% marrow plasma cells. Tell: 1.5 g/dL and 4% are both below those lines.
Active multiple myeloma with end-organ damage
Myeloma needs 10% or more marrow plasma cells or a plasmacytoma plus a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature. Tell: 4% and no end-organ damage rule it out.
ruled out by a stated finding
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoma producing immunoglobulin M with hyperviscosity. Tell: no immunoglobulin M or hyperviscosity is given; the numbers fit the low-level plasma cell disorder.

Correct. An M-protein below 3 g/dL (1.5 g/dL), clonal marrow plasma cells below 10% (4%) and no myeloma-defining characteristics meet every part of MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance), which progresses at about 1% per year.

set1.q: Under the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System), a myeloma patient who meets neither stage I nor stage III criteria is which stage?
opts: Stage I requires every favorable criterion: beta-2 microglobulin under 3.5 mg/L, albumin at least 3.5 g/dL, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: missing stage I makes it II or III.

Correct. In the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System), stage II is defined as not stage I or III. Stage I needs low beta-2 microglobulin, normal albumin, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase; stage III needs high beta-2 microglobulin with high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase.
Stage III requires beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more with high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: not meeting stage III leaves stage II.
The R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) has only three stages. Tell: the stages are I, II and III.

set1.q: Why are many patients expected to die with chronic lymphocytic leukemia rather than from it?
opts: Spontaneous regression is not described; asymptomatic disease is watched until rapid progression or symptoms. Tell: the reasons are age at onset and novel therapies.
Survival improved because of novel agents rather than historical chemotherapy, and pill therapy may be indefinite. Tell: control with modern agents in older patients, not a one-course cure.
The disease involves the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Tell: the favorable outlook comes from elderly onset and novel agents, not from sparing the marrow.

Correct. Ongoing development of novel therapies (such as cellular and bispecific antibody therapies) and the elderly age at onset, median 70 years, mean many patients will die with chronic lymphocytic leukemia rather than from it.

set1.q: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma is strongly associated with which virus?
opts: Hepatitis C is associated with splenic marginal zone lymphoma. Tell: the endemic Burkitt virus is Epstein-Barr.
Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 is linked to adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Tell: Burkitt is a B-cell lymphoma tied to Epstein-Barr virus.

Correct. Endemic Burkitt lymphoma, seen largely in sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea, is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus. The sporadic type is seen in the United States and Western Europe, and the third type with immunodeficiency.
Human immunodeficiency virus is linked to the immunodeficiency-associated type, not the endemic type. Tell: endemic is the African type, linked to Epstein-Barr virus.

set1.q: Which is a poor prognostic factor in non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
opts: T-cell lymphomas respond less well than B-cell lymphomas, so a B-cell type is not the adverse factor. Tell: T-cell is worse.

Correct. Poor prognostic factors are age over 60, extranodal sites, poor performance status (an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group grade above 2), stage III or IV disease and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase.
Age over 60 is the poor prognostic factor in non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: younger age is favorable.
Stage III or IV, not stage I, predicts a poor prognosis. Tell: localized disease is favorable.

set1.q: How is early, non-bulky stage I or II Hodgkin lymphoma without B symptoms treated?
opts: Watch and wait suits asymptomatic chronic lymphocytic leukemia or follicular lymphoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: early Hodgkin is treated, briefly.
Allogeneic stem cell transplant may be required after relapse following first-line therapy. Tell: transplant is for relapse, not early disease.

Correct. Early stage I and stage II Hodgkin lymphoma without bulk or B symptoms is treated with a short course of chemotherapy, historically ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine). Bulky disease or B symptoms add radiation.
Chemotherapy plus radiation is for bulky stage I or II disease or B symptoms. Tell: early, non-bulky disease without B symptoms needs chemotherapy alone, short course.

opts: Jewish and Eastern European descent are tied to chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: myeloma's race risk is African American.
The Caribbean is where adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is more common. Tell: myeloma's higher-risk group is African American.
New Guinea and sub-Saharan Africa are where endemic Burkitt lymphoma is seen. Tell: myeloma's race risk is African American.

opts: Correct. MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) carries a risk of myeloma progression of about 1% per year. Smoldering myeloma progresses faster, about 10% per year.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma. Tell: smoldering is 10%; the earlier, lower-risk state is about 1%.

set1.q: What is needed to assign a Rai stage in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Rai staging does not require advanced imaging; it can be performed with the physical exam and labs, by checking for lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, anemia and thrombocytopenia alongside the lymphocytosis.
Rai staging does not require advanced imaging. Computed tomography or positron emission tomography is used to stage lymphomas. Tell: Rai is a bedside-plus-blood-count staging system.
A marrow biopsy is not needed for Rai staging and is usually not needed for diagnosis either. Tell: the stage comes from the exam and the blood counts.
Cytogenetics inform prognosis and some treatment choices but are not part of the Rai stage. Tell: Rai uses nodes, organs, hemoglobin and platelets, not chromosomes.

opts: Twice is the male excess in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, not the Hodgkin sibling risk. Tell: Hodgkin sibling risk is tenfold.
Four times understates the sibling risk, which is 10 times. Tell: the same-sex sibling figure is ten.
Correct. Same-sex siblings of a patient have a 10 times increased risk of also developing Hodgkin lymphoma. Epstein-Barr virus is a suspected risk factor, found in 40-50% of cases.

opts: Primary care can manage it alone
Myeloma requires referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a myeloma expert. Tell: specialist care is required.

Correct. Myeloma treatment is likely lifelong, with periods of remission (disease control) followed by worsening symptoms, and life-long follow-up for lab monitoring. Care is by a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a myeloma expert.
One course of therapy cures it
Myeloma is currently considered incurable, although that may change during the patient's life. Tell: lifelong treatment, not a single course.
Life-long follow-ups for lab monitoring and treatment are required. Tell: remission is followed by relapse, so monitoring continues.

set1.q: Which chromosomal translocation causes follicular lymphoma?
opts: The t(14;16) translocation is another high-risk abnormality in the myeloma staging table. Tell: myeloma lists 4;14 and 14;16; follicular lymphoma is 14;18.

Correct. Follicular lymphoma arises from the t(14;18) translocation, which places the B-cell lymphoma 2 gene on chromosome 14 and prevents cell death. Microscopy often shows clusters of packed follicles.
The t(11;14) translocation of the cyclin D1 gene identifies mantle cell lymphoma, an aggressive type. Tell: 11;14 is mantle cell; 14;18 is follicular.
The t(4;14) translocation is a high-risk chromosomal abnormality in the myeloma staging table. Tell: it belongs to multiple myeloma, not to a lymphoma.

set1.q: Which agent used in chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor?
opts: Venetoclax is the B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, combined with monoclonal antibodies for a fixed duration. Tell: the kinase inhibitors end in -brutinib.
Obinutuzumab is a monoclonal antibody, listed with rituximab and ofatumumab. Tell: monoclonal antibodies end in -mab; the kinase inhibitors end in -brutinib.
Allopurinol is a hypouricemic agent given with fluids before aggressive lymphoma treatment to prevent tumor lysis syndrome. Tell: it prevents a complication; it is not a targeted leukemia therapy.

Correct. The Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors are ibrutinib, acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib, usually given continuously when used as monotherapy. They are one of the targeted therapies for chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

set1.q: About 80% of chronic lymphocytic leukemia cases arise from one of four chromosomal changes. Which is one of them?
opts: The t(14;18) translocation places the B-cell lymphoma 2 gene on chromosome 14 and prevents cell death in follicular lymphoma. Tell: chronic lymphocytic leukemia changes are deletions or a trisomy, not this translocation.
The t(11;14) translocation of the cyclin D1 gene identifies mantle cell lymphoma. Tell: the four chronic lymphocytic leukemia changes are deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12 and deletion 17p.

The t(4;14) translocation is a high-risk chromosomal abnormality in the myeloma staging table, not one of the four chronic lymphocytic leukemia changes. Tell: myeloma high-risk changes are translocations plus deletion 17p.

Correct. About 80% of cases result from loss or addition of chromosomal material in one of four abnormalities: deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12 and deletion 17p. These are why cytogenetics matters for prognosis.

set1.q: Which disorder produces an immunoglobulin M monoclonal protein and is separated from multiple myeloma in the differential?
opts: Amyloidosis is another disorder with a paraprotein in the differential, but immunoglobulin M production is the Waldenstrom signature. Tell: M means Waldenstrom.
Correct. Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia often produces an immunoglobulin M monoclonal protein, with a different pathophysiology and treatment from myeloma, which most commonly makes immunoglobulin G.
Smoldering myeloma is an intermediate plasma cell disorder on the path to myeloma, often monitored. Tell: the immunoglobulin M producer is Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

set1.q: Which delayed toxicity can follow Hodgkin lymphoma treatment?
opts: Hyperviscosity is caused by immunoglobulin M in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: the delayed Hodgkin toxicities are myelodysplastic syndrome, secondary leukemia and other cancers.
Erythroderma is the widespread red itchy rash of Sezary syndrome. Tell: Hodgkin treatment's late harms are new marrow cancers.
Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma treatment may have delayed toxicities, including myelodysplastic syndrome, secondary leukemia and other cancers. Bleomycin also carries pulmonary toxicity.

Osteoclast activation releases calcium into the blood and causes the hypercalcemia and bone lesions. Tell: osteoclasts explain calcium and bone, not the kidney.

Phosphorus is released and, as calcium phosphate crystals, contributes to acute renal failure, but the largest risk is from potassium. Tell: the killer is the arrhythmia of hyperkalemia.

Plasma cells of 10-60% with a monoclonal protein above 3 g/dL and no myeloma-defining event is smoldering myeloma. Tell: without a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature it is smoldering, not myeloma.

set2.q: If Hodgkin lymphoma relapses after first-line treatment, what may be required?

Autologous transplant with maintenance therapy improves survival in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma. Tell: for Hodgkin lymphoma relapsing after first-line treatment, the transplant named is allogeneic.

Fifteen percent is the T-cell or natural killer-cell share, not the B-cell share. Tell: B-cell lymphomas are the large majority.
The split is not even; B-cell types make up about 85%. Tell: the T-cell and natural killer-cell types are the minority at 15%.

Allopurinol is a hypouricemic agent to prevent tumor lysis syndrome, not a lymphoma therapy. Tell: it protects the kidneys; rituximab treats the lymphoma.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated in aggressive lymphoma, and patients are given allopurinol (a hypouricemic agent) and fluids in advance. Patients are told to drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol on starting treatment.

A fixed duration describes venetoclax combined with monoclonal antibodies. Tell: kinase inhibitor monotherapy keeps going.

opts: Clonal plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, define the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: plasma cells make a monoclonal protein; this leukemia is a lymphocytosis of mature B cells.

Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a proliferative leukemia of mature B-cell lymphocytes found in the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Mutagenesis occurs in mature B cells, which is why the disease presents as a clonal population.
Immature blasts describe an acute leukemia, not this chronic disease, whose cells are mature B lymphocytes. Tell: chronic means mature cells accumulating; acute means blasts.

Mature T-cell leukemias exist but are rare and carry another name, T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia itself is a B-cell disease. Tell: the common chronic lymphocytic leukemia is B-cell; the T-cell form is rare and named separately.

set2.q: Which organ enlargement is most often found on exam in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: A nasal-region mass points to extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: this leukemia enlarges the spleen in about 40%.

Correct. On exam, splenomegaly is found in about 40% of patients, while hepatomegaly is less common. Organ enlargement also moves the Rai stage to II when lymphocytosis and lymphadenopathy are present.
Hepatomegaly can occur but is less common than splenomegaly (about 40%). Tell: the spleen is the organ enlarged most often here.

A mediastinal mass on chest X-ray is a feature of Hodgkin lymphoma and of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma, not the usual exam finding here. Tell: a chest mass suggests a lymphoma; the spleen is the organ that enlarges in this leukemia.

set2.q: What is the goal of treatment in multiple myeloma?
opts: Long remissions and quality of life
Correct. Because myeloma is by definition symptomatic and considered incurable, the goal of treatment is maintaining prolonged remissions to improve survival while maintaining quality of life.
Myeloma is considered incurable, and each line of therapy gives shorter remissions. Tell: the aim is long remission, not cure.
Myeloma is by definition symptomatic; observation fits smoldering myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy. Tell: active myeloma is treated.
Eradication is not the stated aim; the disease remains incurable and relapsing. Tell: prolong remission, protect quality of life.

set2.q: Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal incidence. Which two age groups are affected?
opts: The peaks are earlier: adults in their 20s and adults over 60. Tell: one peak in young adulthood, one past 60.
The younger peak in the 20s is right, but the second is in adults over 60, not the 40s. Tell: the older peak is past 60.
Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal incidence, peaking in adults in their 20s and in adults over 60 years old. Older patients also have inferior results with treatment.
Early childhood is not one of the peaks; the younger peak is adults in their 20s. Tell: young adults, not toddlers.

set2.q: What causes the hypercalcemia of multiple myeloma?
opts: Light chain and calcium phosphate deposition cause the renal dysfunction of myeloma, not the hypercalcemia. Tell: light chains hit the kidney; osteoclasts release the calcium.
Tumor lysis releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid, not calcium from bone. Tell: myeloma calcium comes from bone resorption.
Renal dysfunction in myeloma comes from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition; the calcium itself comes from bone. Tell: osteoclasts are the source.

Correct. Myeloma activates osteoclasts, resulting in calcium release into the bloodstream. Hypercalcemia causes constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency and nausea, and the same bone resorption makes punched-out lesions.

set2.q: In the Rai classification, lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, with normal hemoglobin and platelets, is which stage?
opts: Stage I is lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy only. Tell: an enlarged spleen counts as organomegaly and moves the stage to II.
Correct. Rai stage II is lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy and organomegaly, defined as hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly. With no anemia and no thrombocytopenia, the stage does not rise to III or IV.
Stage III requires anemia. Tell: the hemoglobin is normal, so organomegaly alone stops at stage II.
Stage IV requires thrombocytopenia. Tell: the platelets are normal, so the stage cannot reach IV.

set2.q: What is the median age at diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Forty is far too young for the median; chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a disease of older adults with a median age of 70 years. Tell: think of an older adult found on routine blood work, not a young adult.
Fifty-five falls well short of the median age of 70 years for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the median sits a decade above 60, not below it.

Correct. The median age at diagnosis, and at onset, of chronic lymphocytic leukemia is 70 years, so it is a disease of older adults. That elderly onset is one reason many patients are expected to die with the disease rather than from it.
Eighty-five overshoots; the median age at diagnosis is 70 years. Tell: the median is 70, so half of patients are diagnosed younger than that.

set2.q: What share of chronic lymphocytic leukemia patients develop B symptoms?
opts: Correct. Only 5-10% of patients develop B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers). Most are diagnosed while asymptomatic, and painless lymphadenopathy (50-90%) is far more frequent.
About 40% is the frequency of splenomegaly on exam, not of B symptoms. Tell: B symptoms are uncommon, at 5-10%.
Fifty to 90% is the frequency of painless lymphadenopathy in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, not of B symptoms. Tell: nodes are common; B symptoms are rare at 5-10%.

Seventy percent is the share of Hodgkin lymphoma patients with painless asymptomatic lymphadenopathy, not of B symptoms in chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: B symptoms here are a small minority, 5-10%.

set2.q: What is the typical presentation of follicular lymphoma?
opts: Node pain that worsens with alcohol is a Hodgkin lymphoma feature. Tell: alcohol-linked pain points to Hodgkin; follicular nodes are painless and fluctuate in size.
A widespread red itchy rash (erythroderma) is Sezary syndrome, the aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Tell: skin disease means a T-cell lymphoma; follicular lymphoma presents with nodes.
Correct. Follicular lymphoma typically has an indolent presentation with waxing and waning painless lymphadenopathy. It is the most common indolent histology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Swelling that visibly grows over one day is Burkitt lymphoma, a very aggressive variant. Tell: day-to-day growth means Burkitt; waxing and waning means follicular.

set2.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required to diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the blood itself is examined by flow cytometry to show the clone.

Excisional lymph node biopsy is how a lymphoma is diagnosed, because the node architecture must be seen. This leukemia is confirmed from the blood. Tell: node biopsy is for lymphoma; flow cytometry is for this leukemia.

Serum protein electrophoresis shows the monoclonal protein of multiple myeloma and the other plasma cell disorders. Tell: a monoclonal protein means a plasma cell disorder; a clonal B-cell population on flow means chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry, which identifies the clonal B-cell population, coexpressing the cluster of differentiation markers 19 and 5. A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required.

set2.q: How is venetoclax typically given in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Radiation is used for a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not combined with venetoclax. Tell: venetoclax pairs with a monoclonal antibody.
Maintenance therapy after autologous transplant improves survival in multiple myeloma. Tell: transplant maintenance belongs to myeloma; venetoclax is a time-limited combination here.
With an antibody, for a fixed time

Correct. Venetoclax, the B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, is combined with monoclonal antibodies for a fixed duration. That contrasts with Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which are usually continuous when used alone.
Continuous monotherapy describes the Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as ibrutinib. Tell: venetoclax is paired with an antibody and given for a set time.

set2.q: Mantle cell lymphoma is identified by which translocation?
opts: The t(14;18) translocation places the B-cell lymphoma 2 gene on chromosome 14 in follicular lymphoma. Tell: 14;18 is follicular; 11;14 is mantle cell.
The t(4;14) translocation is a high-risk abnormality in the myeloma staging table. Tell: it marks high-risk myeloma, not a lymphoma.
The t(14;16) translocation is a high-risk myeloma abnormality. Tell: mantle cell lymphoma is the cyclin D1 translocation, 11;14.

Correct. Mantle cell lymphoma is a rare subtype identified by the cyclin D1 gene translocation t(11;14). It typically has an aggressive course, is more common in men and has a median age of 60-70 years.
